newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angola has no plans to invade Zaire, firms told.
newsitem.headline: Angola has no plans to invade Zaire, firms told.

text.p: Angola's military has given assurances it has no plans to invade neighbouring Zaire to back rebels fighting to topple President Mobutu Sese Seko, foreign companies in the oil-rich Cabinda enclave say.

Company representatives in Cabinda, which is separated from the rest of Angola by a stretch of Zaire territory, expressed cocern over their investments after reports that Angolan troops had invaded Zaire to the south.

One company official however, quoted the Angolan regional army commander for Cabinda as saying the situation was normal. "General (Luis) Mendes said he went down to the border and said everything was normal. He said the reports were false," the official said.

The Luanda government denied on Saturday charges by the Kinshasa government that Angolan troops had crossed into Zaire from Cabinda. Angolan presidential spokesman Aldemiro Vaz de Conceicao denied there were any of his country's troops in Zaire.
The Mobutu government said Angolan troops had invaded Yema village, close to Muanda on the Atlantic coast, with 1,400 troops. It also reported Angolan troops were around Tshikapa further inland.
Most foreign oil companies active in Angola have onshore bases in Cabinda to support offshore drilling operations.

U.S.-based Chevron, for example, is one of the largest operating in Angola and has embarked on an expansion of its operations. Its subsidiary The Cabinda Gulf Oil Company operates offshore the enclave with partners such as the Angolan state oil company Sonangol, French-based Total, Agip of Italy and Portugal's Petrogal.

Expatriate mining officials in Angola's northeastern Lunda Norte province said on Friday the Angolan army and Zaire rebels were performing joint military exercises on the Angolan side of the border at Dundo.

Western diplomats in Luanda said any Angolan military activity might be linked more to a desire to act against FLEC separatist guerrillas who have been fighting for years for independence for Cabinda.
The diplomats say the guerrillas have bases in Zaire to the south and southeast of Cabinda.
The guerrillas, divided into 13 factions, were not party to a 1994 ceasefire agreement between the Angolan government and the country's former UNITA rebels to end two decades of civil war.
"It is much more likely that the government wants to move against the FLEC, than invade Zaire in an attempt to cut off Kinshasa for the rebels from its only seaport at Matadi," one diplomat said.
The Luanda government has been linked to Zaire rebel leader Laurent Kabila's campaign to topple the ailing Mobutu at least partly because Mobutu was a strong ally of UNITA.

UNITA held supply bases in Zaire during the Angolan war, but these have since been closed as the forces of Zaire rebel leader Laurent Kabila have taken control of more than half of the country since he launched his seven-month rebellion.
